caseno:
Criminal Revision No. 848 of 1991 (Dhaka)
Criminal Revision No. 52 of 1989 (Comilla)
lawyer:
Harunur Rashid, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Md. Abdul Aziz, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Party No.1.
parties:
Abdul Malek ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Payer Ahmed Chowdhury and State ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Karim,J.:This Rule on an application under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was issued calling upon the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla, and opposite party No. 1 Payer Ahmed Chowdhury to show cause as to why the order dated 16.2.89 passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Comilla, in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 479 of 1988 directing further investigation in Nangalkot PS case No. 3 dated 14.5.88 under sections 302/20/427/34 of the Penal Code should not be set aside. 

 2. Opposite party No. 1 Payer Ahmed Chowdhury filed a first information report on 14.5.88 against the petitioner and 24 others with the allegation that accused persons being armed with deadly weapons and forming an unlawful assembly raided his house and caused the death of his mother with a dagger blow and accordingly Nangalkot PS case No.3 dated 14.5.88 under sections 147/148/149 323/302/379/380/447/427/302 of the Penal Code was started against the petitioner and other accused persons, but the police after investigation having found a prima facie case being established against informant Payer Ahmed Chowdhury and his party men for committing the murder of mother of the informant, submitted a Charge-sheet against them under sections 302/201/427/34 of the Penal Code and also submitted a final report against those persons, who were made accused in the first information report lodged by Payer Ahmed Chowdhury. The charge sheet was accepted by the learned Upazila Magistrate, Nangalkot, Comilla, and he discharged the petitioner and other accused persons in respect of whom the final report was filed by the police. Petitioner Abdul Malek also filed a first information report on 16.5.88 under sections 147/148/324/326/376/307/366 along with the provisions of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 against opposite party Payer Ahmed Chowdhury and some other persons for commission of the offence of looting, grievous hurt, rape and other offences and, after investigation, the police submitted charge-sheet against Payer Ahmed Chowdhury and his party men under those sections. This case being Nangalkot PS case No.4 (GR case No. 32 of 1988) is now pending in the Court of the learned Magistrate. Payer Ahmed Chowdhury did not file any naraji petition before the learned Magistrate against the final report submitted by the police in Nangalkot PS Case No. 3 dated 14.5.88, but straightaway filed before the learned Sessions Judge a petition under section (3B) of section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure seeking further investigation by the police in respect of the accused persons about whom the police had submitted a final report in Nangalkot PS case No. 3 dated 14.5.88. The learned Sessions Judge under his order dated 16.2.88 allowed the application in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 479 of 1988 and directed further investigation to be made by the Criminal Investigating Agencies, Bangladesh. Aggrieved by this order of the learned Sessions Judge, the petitioner, who was an accused in Nangalkot PS case No. 3 dated 14.5.88, has preferred this revisional application under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 3. Mr. Harunur-Rashid, learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the order passed by the learned Sessions Judge directing further investigation is without jurisdiction inasmuch as sub-section (3B) of section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not vest the Sessions Judge with any authority to direct further investigation in respect of offence after submission of a final report by the police. He further submits that the remedy available to the informant was to file a naraji petition before the learned Magistrate, which he did not do, and in the instant case, the exercise of power by the learned Sessions Judge under sub-section (3B) of section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is without jurisdiction and illegal and as such, should be set aside. 

 7. Under sub-section(6) of section 167 CrPC the Sessions Judge could, if he was satisfied, on an application made to him or otherwise, direct further investigation in the appropriate case into the offence which was stopped on the expiry either of the specified time or of the extended time under sub-section (5). This sub-section containing a provision for direction of further investigation by the Sessions Judge, was however, omitted by Code of Criminal Procedure (2nd Amendment) Act, 1992. Md. Abdul Aziz, learned Advocate for the opposite party, submits that though Payer Ahmed Chowdhury filed an application before the learned Sessions Judge purporting it to be under section (3B) of section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, it was, in fact an application under section (6) of section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, because at the relevant time when the application was made before the Sessions Judge and was allowed by him, this provision namely, sub-section (6) of section 167 was in the statute book. He submits that this provision was first incorporated in the Code by Ordinance No. 24 of 1982 and was repealed on 1.11.92 by the Code of Criminal Procedure (2nd amendment) Act, 1992. In this view of the matter, Mr. Abdul Aziz submits that the impugned order passed by the Sessions Judge on 16.2.89 directing further investigation by the Criminal Investigation Agencies, Bangladesh was perfectly valid and in accordance with law. 

 (7A) Where an accused has been released under sub-section (7), the case against him shall not be revived after the expiry of six months of the release and for revival of the investigation within the said period of six months, specific order of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or the District Magistrate, as the case may be, shall have to be obtained. 

 Provided that the Government may, by order, revive the case at any time if the case is triable exclusively by Court of Sessions." 

 9. It is clear from a perusal of the provision of sub-section (6) of section 167 that the Sessions Judge had the power of directing further investigation into an offence while it was stopped by the Magistrate on the expiry of specified time or the extended time under sub-section (5). Once this further investigation was stopped by the Magistrate under sub-section (5), the accused had the right to be released forthwith and after such release by the Magistrate it was only the District Magistrate or the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, as the case may be, who had the power of reviving the investigation within a period of six months and this power of revival could not be exercised after the expiry of six months from the date of release. The Government had the authority to revive the case at any time if the case was triable exclusively by the court of sessions. This position was examined by Division Bench of this Court in the case of Md. Abul Kalam Azad Vs. State reported in 38 DLR 159 where it has been held that sub-section (6) of section 167 empowered the Sessions Judge to direct further investigation that was stopped by the Magistrate on the expiry either of the specifed time or of the extended time under sub-section (5). In the instant case further investigation was not stopped by the Magistrate under sub-section (5) of section 167 as a result of which the Sessions Judge had no jurisdiction for directing further investigation. Mr. Harunur Rashid, learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that in the instant case the Magistrate passed an order of discharge of the accused persons on acceptance of the final report and this order of discharge did not operate as an order of stopping further investigation into the offence. After passing an order of discharge, there remains nothing for the police to investigate, nor the Magistrate has anything to do with the case unless the informant files before him a naraji petition. In this case Payer Ahmed Chowdhury did not file any naraji petition against the order of discharge. 

 10. Mr. Abdul Aziz, learned Advocate for the opposite party, has submitted that the Sessions Judge has the authority to direct further investigation after passing an order of discharge by the Magistrate and in support of his contention has referred to the, case of Sher Ali (Md) and others Vs. State reported in 46 DLR (AD) 67=1994 DLD (AD) 84. In this reported case the informant filed a naraji petition against the exclusion of names of some accused persons from the charge-sheet in a case under section 4 of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1992. The Magistrate rejected the naraji petition thereby refusing to direct further investigation. Against this order the informant came to the Sessions Judge in revision under section 439A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Sessions Judge by his order directed that further investigation be held and charge-sheet submitted under section 4 of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1992. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division upheld the direction of the Sessions Judge to hold further investigation by the police as being lawful, but considered the order so far as it relates to submission of the charge-sheet as being without jurisdiction. Relying on "This decision Mr. Abdul Aziz submits that the Sessions Judge has inherent jurisdiction for directing the police for further investigation in the instant case, but the facts of the reported case are distinguishable from those of the instant case where the informant did not file any naraji petition. If the informant had filed a naraji petition and it had been rejected by the Magistrate, it could have been challenged in revision under section 439A of the Code of Criminal Procedure conferring a jurisdiction on the Sessions Judge to direct the police to hold further investigation. This having not been done, the order of the Sessions Judge directing further investigation on an application by the informant is without jurisdiction and is liable to be set aside. 

 In the result, the Rule is made absolute and the impugned order dated 16.2.89 passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Comilla in Criminal Miscellaneous Case NoA79 of 1988 directing further investigation is set aside.
